newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bank chief calls for deficit cut this year.
newsitem.headline: French bank chief calls for deficit cut this year.

text.p: Bank of France chief Jean-Claude Trichet, laying down a challenge to the newly-elected left-wing government, said on Tuesday it was essential to make cuts in public deficits in 1997.
Presenting the bank's annual report at a news conference, Trichet said: "Controlling public spending and reducing public deficits is indispensable in 1997 as it is in the medium term."
The independent central bank's governor said payroll deductions to fund the welfare system were too high and public spending must also fall.
Trichet stressed the report was written before new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin announced his policy programme last week and did not constitute a response to it.

Jospin announced last Thursday a four percent increase in the national minimum wage from July 1 and new spending measures for low-income families and to renovate public housing which economists say will cost at least 10 billion francs this year.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn has said the government does not intend to increase the 1997 deficit and extra spending will be matched by savings elsewhere. But Jospin during his election campaign ruled out further austerity to cut this year's deficit.

Trichet said wage restraint in 1996 had been very important to preserve price stability and keep the French economy competitive. "This moderation remains necessary in the future to fight unemployment," he said.

The bank governor said a total tax burden of 45.7 percent of gross domestic product last year and a ratio of public spending to GDP of 54.7 percent were "manifestly too high" and should be reduced gradually and substantially.
He noted that the European Union public spending average was 49.9 percent and the Group of Seven's average was 39.7 percent.
Spending cuts should cover the full range of the public sector: the state, social security, local authorities and public bodies funded by semi-fiscal taxes.
Trichet said monetary policy had brought French market interest rates to historic lows but was not sufficient to fight unemployment, which required structural reforms and sustained deficit reduction.

"Structural reforms are particularly indispensable concerning employment," the report said, urging the government, employers and trade unions to learn from the examples of other continental European countries which had been more successful than France.

Trichet said market interest rates were low because the franc was stable and credible and vowed the Bank of France would continue its action in 1997-98 to ensure that the euro inspired as much confidence as the franc.
Answering questions, the central bank governor declined to be drawn on Jospin's policies.

"We are not replying to the government's policy statement because this report was written prior to it. But what we are saying ourselves is that if one wants to create jobs, measures must be taken to reinforce competitiveness," he said.
